title: For No Reason?
sum: In the land of Uz lives Job, a man the narrator calls wholehearted and upright, who fears God and keeps away from evil. He has seven sons, three daughters and vast herds, and he is the greatest man of the East. He even offers sacrifices for his children in case they have cursed God in their hearts. Then the scene moves to heaven. The sons of God take their stand before the LORD, and among them comes the Accuser. The LORD points out his servant Job; the Accuser asks whether Job fears God "for no reason," and claims that if God touches what Job has, Job will curse him to his face. The LORD gives him power over everything Job owns, but not over Job himself.

On one day, while his children are feasting, four messengers arrive, each interrupting the last: raiders from Sheba have taken the oxen and donkeys, fire from God has burned the sheep, Chaldeans have taken the camels, and a great wind has brought down the house on Job's sons and daughters. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships: "The LORD gave, and the LORD took. Let the LORD's name be blessed." The narrator closes the first test: Job did not sin, and did not say God had done anything unfitting.
readings: Read as history

Many Jewish and Christian readers take the chapter as an account of real events in the age of the patriarchs, with the heavenly scene as a revelation of what was really happening behind Job's disasters. Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11 speak of Job as a real man, and the detailed names (Uz, Sheba, the Chaldeans) fit a real world. On this reading the chapter teaches that suffering can have causes hidden from the sufferer, and that God sets limits on evil.
Read as a framing tale

Most scholars read chapters 1–2 as a deliberately simple folk story, with its round numbers, repeated scenes, formula speech and messengers who arrive just as the last one finishes. The story poses a question, whether piety can be free, and sets up the poem that follows. The heavenly scene is told to the reader, not to Job, so that the reader knows what Job and his friends never learn: his suffering is not punishment.

views.H: A real patriarchal-age man in a real land east of Israel, whose losses are told as they happened; the heavenly council is a true glimpse of the unseen court, which Job never sees (Andersen, Hartley).
views.C: An old prose tale, perhaps known in Israel before the poem (Ezekiel 14:14), now framing the dialogue. Its features, the Accuser as a member of the court, the round numbers and the repeated scenes, are signs of a crafted narrative, and the Accuser's role suggests a date near Zechariah 3 (Persian period) for the frame in its present form (Clines, Pope, Newsom).
views.W: The Babylonian poem 'I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom' (Ludlul bel nemeqi) also tells of a pious man struck down by losses and illness, abandoned by friends, and in the end restored by the god Marduk. But Ludlul has no heavenly test; its sufferer never learns why he suffered and assumes he must have offended a god unknowingly. Job's prologue gives the reader the reason, and the reason is not sin.
views.J: The rabbis asked when Job lived and whether he was a gentile; one view puts him in the days of Moses, another makes him one of Pharaoh's advisers (Bavli Sotah 11a; Bava Batra 15a–b). The Mishnah concludes from 13:15 and 27:5 that Job served God out of love (Sotah 5:5); the Accuser's 'for no reason' poses the same question. The Talmud also teaches that the Accuser meant well (Bava Batra 16a).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the chapter the boundaries God sets on the devil (compare Luke 22:31–32; 1 Corinthians 10:13) and in 1:21 a model of faith in loss; Gregory the Great reads Job as a figure of Christ and of the church, suffering without guilt. Job's words are read at Christian funerals.

deep.h: What kind of test is this?
deep.b:
The Accuser's charge is not that Job is wicked but that his goodness is for sale: God has "put a fence around him" and blessed him, so of course he fears God (1:10). If that is true of the best man on earth, then religion is a contract, and no one loves God "for no reason." The LORD accepts the challenge, which means that the test is about God's honor as much as Job's: is God worth loving for himself? The test also has strict limits: first property, then the body, never the life (1:12; 2:6).

Readers have long felt the cost of this test. Job's ten children die in it, and the book does not give their deaths their own scene. Traditional readers have answered that God's purposes are larger than one family's tragedy and that the children's lives belonged to God; some add that the restoration of 42:13 is a sign of hope beyond death. Others hold that the prologue is a story-form, not a record of God's real dealings, and that the poem itself protests against any God who would play with lives. The book lets both reactions stand: it begins with the wager and ends with the LORD saying Job spoke rightly about him (42:7).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the Accuser and the friends ask the same question
deep.b: My own suggestion: the Accuser disappears after chapter 2, but his question does not. Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar take it up from the other side. The Accuser assumed that blessing explains goodness; the friends assume that suffering reveals wickedness. Both treat God's dealings with people as a ledger of payment. So the dialogue keeps on trying the Accuser's theory in human form, and the LORD's rebuke of the friends (42:7) answers the Accuser too, though he is never named again. Many scholars, among them Newsom and Clines, note that the friends share the logic of retribution that the prologue questions; linking that logic explicitly to the Accuser's challenge in 1:9–11 is my own reading.

echoes: Ezekiel 14:14; James 5:11; 1 Kings 22:19–22; Zechariah 3:1–2; Genesis 36:28; Lamentations 4:21; Ecclesiastes 5:15; 1 Timothy 6:7; Luke 22:31–32

settings.to: The sons of God gathered in the heavenly court
settings.when: on the day the heavenly beings report to the LORD, while Job, unaware, is at peace on earth
settings.why: The LORD holds up Job as proof that a human being can be wholehearted; the Accuser challenges whether that goodness is free. The dialogue sets the terms of the test and its limit (not Job himself). It is spoken before the court, so the question is public: God's honor and Job's integrity are on trial together.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, likely Judeans after the disaster of 586 BC, the scene told them what Job never learns: suffering is not always punishment, and heaven may be watching how the faithful respond. It also answered fear of a capricious heaven: the Accuser can do nothing without the LORD's word.
views: Traditional readers take it as revelation of the unseen court, as in 1 Kings 22:19–22 and Zechariah 3.
Many scholars take the scene as the storyteller's way of giving readers knowledge that the characters lack, a dramatic irony that drives the whole book.

settings.when: on the day his children are feasting in the oldest brother's house
settings.why: Each messenger reports one disaster and his own escape, in nearly the same words, and each arrives before the last has finished. The reports leave Job no time to recover between blows, and their repeated ending, 'only I got away, just me, to tell you,' stresses how total the loss is.
settings.readers: The rapid, formulaic reports let readers feel the shock as Job felt it, and the pattern of human enemies and natural forces from every direction shows that no part of life was safe. For readers who had survived war and exile, the lone survivors' voices would have been familiar.

settings.to: Spoken before God, with the surviving messengers present
settings.when: just after the news of his children's deaths, as he lies face down in mourning
settings.why: Job confesses that he came into the world with nothing and will leave with nothing, that everything he had was the LORD's to give and to take, and he blesses the LORD's name. The words answer the Accuser's prediction directly: Job blesses God instead of cursing him.
settings.readers: Job's saying gave Israel words for grief that hold on to God without pretending the loss is small. It became part of Jewish and Christian burial prayers. Notice that Job names the LORD as the one who took, not the raiders: he does not explain his loss away.

traditions.q: Is the satan of Job the devil?
views: Yes: the Accuser is the devil, a fallen angel whose power is real but limited, who can act only by God's permission (Catechism 391–395; Gregory the Great's Moralia; Aquinas on Job).
Yes: Calvin preaches the prologue as Satan's assault on Job, held on God's leash and serving God's purpose (Sermons on Job).

Divided: many identify him with Satan, reading Job with Revelation 12:9–10; others, such as John Walton, argue that the satan of Job is a member of the heavenly court acting as a challenger or prosecutor, not yet the devil of later Scripture, and that the article marks a role, not a name.
Yes: Satan the Devil, a real spirit person, who in Job challenged whether humans would keep integrity to God from unselfish motives; Job's faithfulness is part of God's answer to that challenge.

title: Skin for Skin
sum: The heavenly court gathers again. The LORD repeats his praise of Job, adding that Job still holds on to his integrity although the Accuser lured him to ruin Job "for no reason." The Accuser answers with a proverb, "Skin for skin!": touch the man's own body and he will curse God. The LORD gives Job's body into his hand but tells him to keep Job's life safe. The Accuser strikes Job with bad boils from head to foot, and Job sits in the ashes scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery.

His wife says, "Still holding on to your integrity? Curse God, and die." Job answers that she talks like a godless woman: should we take good from God and not bad? "Through all this Job did not sin with his lips." Then three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, come from their homes to comfort him. They do not recognize him; they weep, tear their robes, throw dust over their heads and sit with him on the ground for seven days and nights, saying nothing, because they see how great his pain is.
readings: Read as the end of a patient man's story

On this reading, chapter 2 completes the portrait of the patient Job of James 5:11: twice tested, twice faithful. Job's wife is the last temptation, and his answer is the summit of faith: God is God in good and in bad. What follows in chapter 3 is a lament, but the Job of chapter 2 is the measure of the book.
Read as the hinge to the poem

Many scholars stress the small change from 1:22 to 2:10, 'did not sin with his lips,' and the silent week. Something in Job has been stretched to breaking, and the seven days of silence are the pause before the dam breaks. The friends' silence is their best moment; once they speak, their comfort turns to accusation.

views.H: The second test and the friends' visit are told as events: Job's illness, his wife's words and the arrival of three real men from Teman, Shuah and Naamah.
views.C: The second heavenly scene repeats the first with variations, a classic storytelling pattern. The three friends link the prose tale to the poem; some think the friends were added to an older tale when the dialogue was written, since the prose ending again mentions them (42:7–9).
views.W: In Ludlul the sufferer's family and friends turn away; in the Babylonian Theodicy a friend argues with the sufferer. Job's friends first come to share his grief, an act of loyalty that the Near Eastern texts rarely describe so movingly.
views.J: The Talmud's Rava says Job did not sin 'with his lips,' but sinned in his heart (Bava Batra 16a). The Targum and the Talmud name Job's wife Dinah, daughter of Jacob (Bava Batra 15b). The friends' seven silent days are a model for comforting mourners (Moed Katan 28b).
views.X: Job's wife has often been cast as the devil's helper, though modern Christian readers also see her as a grieving mother. Job's 'Should we take the good from God, and not take the bad too?' is a classic text on accepting suffering, and the friends' silence is often held up as the best ministry to the grieving.

deep.h: Why did the friends sit in silence?
deep.b: Seven days is the time of mourning for the dead (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13), and the friends treat Job as a mourner, perhaps even as a man as good as dead. In the Near East, then and now, visitors to a house of mourning sat with the bereaved and waited. Their silence also has a reason the text gives: "they could see how terrible his pain was" (2:13). Pain that great makes words small. Jewish law took from this verse and from 3:1–4:1 the rule that comforters wait for the mourner to speak first (Bavli Moed Katan 28b). Many readers think the friends' silence was the wisest thing they did, and that their trouble began when they started to explain.

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:35; Exodus 9:8–11; 2 Kings 20:7; 1 Samuel 25:25; Psalm 14:1; Genesis 36:11; Jeremiah 49:7; Genesis 50:10; Ezekiel 3:15; James 5:11

settings.to: The sons of God gathered in the heavenly court
settings.when: after Job has lost everything and still blessed God
settings.why: The LORD declares that the first test has proved Job's integrity and admits that it was 'for no reason'; the Accuser raises the stakes from property to the body. The LORD sets a new limit: Job's life. The scene widens the test and shows that even the most personal suffering lies within the LORD's limits.
settings.readers: First readers learned that Job's illness, like his losses, came by permission inside a divine limit, not as punishment. The LORD's admission that the Accuser 'lured' him to strike Job 'for no reason' would have startled them, as it startled the rabbis, and prepared them to hear Job's complaints as something other than rebellion.

settings.when: after his illness has set in; the Greek says a long time later
settings.why: She questions the integrity God praised and urges Job to curse God, which would bring death and end his agony. Whether she speaks as a tempter or out of despair, her words put the Accuser's prediction into a human voice that Job loves.
settings.readers: Readers heard the test come not from an enemy but from the closest person in Job's life. Ancient readers were divided about her: the Greek gave her a mother's lament; others saw the devil's helper. Either way, she voices the temptation of every sufferer to give God up.
views: Many traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, see her as Satan's tool, the one thing he left Job (Augustine, Calvin).
Others, following the Greek, hear despair and love: she wants Job's suffering to end and has lost her children too.

settings.why: Job rejects her advice as the talk of the godless but includes her in his question, 'should we take the good from God, and not take the bad too?' He holds that God is free to give and to withhold and that faith does not depend on what it receives.
settings.readers: For readers who had received both good and catastrophe from the hand of God, the line gave a confession to hold: God is not a vending machine. It also prepared them for chapter 3, where Job's lips will open.

traditions.q: Does God send suffering like Job's, or only permit it?
views: God never wills evil, but permits it and is able to bring good out of it; the suffering of the innocent can become a share in Christ's redemptive suffering. John Paul II treats Job as the classic case: his suffering is not punishment but a test (Salvifici Doloris 11; Catechism 309–314).

Nothing happens by bare permission: God governs all things, including Satan's acts, for his own holy ends, while the evil remains the guilt of those who do it (Calvin, Institutes 1.18.1; Westminster Confession 5.4).

God permits suffering in a world where creatures are free, and works through it for good; Wesleyans stress that God is not the author of evil and that his love, not his decree, is the key to his dealings with Job.

Divided: classical Pentecostals affirm God's sovereignty in Job's trial and also that healing is part of the gospel (Assemblies of God Fundamental Truths 12); some Word of Faith teachers argue that sickness is never God's will and that Job's fear (3:25) let Satan in, a reading most Pentecostal scholars reject.

title: Let the Day Be Lost
sum: After seven days of silence, Job opens his mouth and curses his day. He wishes the day of his birth and the night of his conception could be wiped out of the calendar: let darkness reclaim them, let no star shine and no dawn come, let those who curse days and rouse Leviathan curse them. Then he asks why he did not die at birth: he would be at rest now in the quiet of the dead, where kings and stillborn babies lie side by side, prisoners hear no driver, and slaves are free.

Finally he asks why light and life are given to the miserable, who long for death and dig for it like treasure, to a man whose road is hidden and whom God has fenced in. Sighs are his bread and roars his drink; what he dreaded has come. He ends: no ease, no quiet, no rest; only turmoil. God is mentioned only in passing; Job does not yet speak to him.
readings: Read as a lament

Job's curse belongs with the laments of the Psalms and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:14–18; Psalm 88), which pour out despair before God without being condemned. He curses his day, not God, and he never threatens to take his own life. God's final verdict that Job spoke rightly (42:7) includes this chapter.
Read as un-creation

The poem runs creation backward: 'let there be darkness' answers 'let there be light' (Genesis 1:3), and Job calls on the powers of chaos to swallow his day. Read this way, chapter 3 is not only grief but a challenge to the order of the world, and the LORD's speeches from the storm, which return to the morning of creation (38:4–12), are its answer (Fishbane, Habel).

views.H: The words of a real man in agony after a week of silence; their extremity measures his pain.
views.C: The opening poem of the dialogue, carefully built in three parts (3:3–10 curse, 3:11–19 why not die, 3:20–26 why live), probably drawing on Jeremiah 20:14–18 and the pattern of Genesis 1 (Fishbane). It marks the shift from the patient Job of the tale to the protesting Job of the poem.
views.W: The Egyptian 'Dispute of a Man with His Ba' contains a famous poem in which death is longed for like recovery from illness, like the smell of myrrh, like a home after captivity. Job 3 shares that longing, but sets the cry within a reversal of creation.
views.J: The rabbis noted the change from the Job of chapters 1–2: some judged that Job here begins to rebel; others that a man may not be held responsible for words spoken in such pain (Bava Batra 16b: 'a person is not held responsible in his distress'). Rashi explains the 'day-cursers' as people who curse their own days in their anguish.
views.X: Christian writers have often read Job 3 as a warning against despair, while also finding in it permission to lament honestly. Gregory the Great reads the curse spiritually: Job curses the day of sin. Many modern pastors use the chapter to show that faith can speak in the language of darkness.

deep.h: Is Job's wish for death a sin?
deep.b: Job wishes he had never been born, asks why he did not die at birth, and envies those who find the grave (3:11, 21–22). Readers have judged this in different ways. Some rabbis and some Christian moralists saw here the first step of Job's fall from patience. Others note that Job's wish is close to Jeremiah's (Jeremiah 20:14–18), Elijah's (1 Kings 19:4) and Jonah's (Jonah 4:3), that he never considers ending his own life, and that God, who rebukes the friends, does not rebuke this lament (42:7). The Talmud preserves a principle often applied to Job: "a person is not held responsible for what he says in his distress" (Bavli Bava Batra 16b). See also the topic on suicide.

echoes: Jeremiah 20:14–18; Genesis 1:3; Jeremiah 4:23–26; Psalm 88; Ecclesiastes 4:2–3; Isaiah 14:9–11; Exodus 5:6; 1 Kings 19:4

Dispute between a man and his Ba

settings.what: Job curses his day and longs for death
settings.to: No one directly: spoken aloud in the presence of his three friends, about his day, about the dead and about God, but not to God
settings.when: after seven days and nights of silent mourning, as the first words of the dialogue
settings.why: Job pours out the full weight of his pain, wishing his birth undone and asking why the suffering are kept alive. He does not curse God, but he refuses the comfort of silence and sets the tone for the debate: his life as it is makes no sense. The friends hear it as dangerous talk and feel they must answer.
settings.readers: For Israelites who had seen their own 'day' turned to darkness, Job's curse gave language to despair without abandoning God. Its echoes of Genesis 1 and of Egyptian slavery (3:18) told them that a sufferer may feel creation and exodus undone, and still be the LORD's servant.
views: Most readers hear a lament like those of the Psalms and Jeremiah, the honest prayer of the suffering.
Some traditional readers saw the beginning of Job's sin of speech, which the friends rightly opposed and God later corrects (38:2).

title: A Voice in the Night
sum: Eliphaz the Temanite, probably the oldest of the friends, speaks first. He begins gently: Job has strengthened many who were stumbling; now trouble has touched him, and he falls apart. Should not his fear of God and his wholehearted ways give him hope? Then he states the rule of his world: no innocent man has ever perished; those who plow wickedness reap it, and God's breath finishes them, as the fiercest lions starve and lose their teeth.

Eliphaz backs his teaching with a revelation. In the night, amid troubling visions, a message stole up to him: a breath passed his face, his hair stood up, a shape stood before him, and in a hush a voice asked, "Is any mortal in the right in God's sight?" If God finds fault even in his angels, how much more in humans, who live in houses of clay and are crushed like a moth, dying without wisdom.
readings: Read as wise counsel

Eliphaz is courteous and draws on real truths: God is just, sin has consequences, no human is pure before God (Psalm 143:2). His counsel is what many pastors would say, and much of it is quoted in Scripture elsewhere (1 Corinthians 3:19 quotes Job 5:13). Read this way, his fault is not falsehood but misapplication: he fits Job to a rule that does not fit him.
Read as a deceptive revelation

Some readers take Eliphaz's night vision as the poet's warning against religious experience used as a weapon. The spirit's message, that no one is righteous before God, contradicts the LORD's verdict on Job (1:8), and its eerie, unnamed source is never confirmed. Job later says his own nights bring terrors, not wisdom (7:14).

views.H: The speech of a real elder of Teman to his suffering friend, recalling a real experience in the night.
views.C: The first speech of the first round. Eliphaz's voice is that of traditional wisdom and of prophetic revelation combined; many scholars see the poet's skill in giving the friends strong, even beautiful, arguments. Some (Tur-Sinai and others) have proposed that 4:12–21 originally belonged to one of Job's speeches, but most keep it with Eliphaz.
views.W: In the Babylonian Theodicy the sufferer's friend also argues that the gods' ways are hard to understand and that humans are inclined to wrong; in the Sumerian poem 'A Man and His God' the sufferer is told that no child has ever been born without sin. Eliphaz's claim that no mortal is pure before God has close Mesopotamian parallels.
views.J: Rabbinic readers sometimes treat Eliphaz with respect as one of the gentile prophets (Bava Batra 15b lists the friends among the prophets of the nations). Maimonides reads him as the view that suffering is always deserved punishment (Guide 3.23).
views.X: Christians have used 4:17 to teach that no one is righteous before God apart from grace (compare Romans 3:10), while also noting that Eliphaz misjudges Job. Gregory the Great reads the friends as heretics who speak much truth but use it badly.

deep.b: The vision of 4:12–16 is told with rare detail: a word coming by stealth; disturbing thoughts in the hours of deep sleep; dread and trembling; a breath on the face; hair standing up; a figure seen but not made out; a hush; a voice. It echoes the great revelations of Scripture, Abram's deep sleep and dread (Genesis 15:12), Elijah's voice of thin silence (1 Kings 19:12). Yet nothing in the text says that the LORD sent it. Its message has two parts: humans cannot be righteous before God (4:17), and they die without wisdom (4:21). The first is true as a general statement; the LORD himself said Job was upright, though, so as a judgment on Job it misfires. Some readers think Eliphaz heard a true word and drew the wrong conclusion; others that the poet wants us to doubt any revelation that serves to silence a sufferer. Elihu returns to God's warnings in dreams in 33:15–18.

echoes: Psalm 37:25; Proverbs 22:8; Galatians 6:7; Genesis 15:12; 1 Kings 19:12; Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:10; 2 Corinthians 5:1; 15:14–16; 25:4–6

settings.to: Job, in front of Bildad and Zophar
settings.when: right after Job's curse of his day, as the first of the friends to answer
settings.why: Eliphaz wants to steady Job and bring him back to hope. He reminds Job of his own past counsel, appeals to the rule that the innocent are never destroyed, cites a night revelation that no human is pure before God, and urges Job to seek God and accept his discipline, promising restoration. His words also correct Job: complaining, he warns, is how fools destroy themselves (5:2).
settings.readers: First readers knew this teaching: it was the wisdom of their own sages and the hope of many psalms. Hearing it applied to a man the reader knows to be innocent, they were made to ask whether their own tradition could explain their nation's suffering, and whether comfort that blames the sufferer is comfort at all.
views: Many readers see Eliphaz as a sincere, gentle friend who applies true principles to the wrong case (Clines, Andersen).
Others hear veiled charges from the start, in 4:7–8 and 5:4, which Eliphaz states openly in chapter 22 (Newsom, Habel).

settings.by: An unnamed spirit or voice, as Eliphaz reports it
settings.to: Eliphaz, alone, in a night vision
settings.when: at some time before these events, in the hours of deep sleep
settings.why: The voice declares that no mortal can be righteous or pure before God, since God finds error even in his angels, and that humans, frail as clay and moths, perish without wisdom. Eliphaz cites it to give his teaching the authority of revelation.
settings.readers: Readers would have heard the language of prophetic visions and asked whether it carried God's authority. The book never confirms the source, and the LORD's praise of Job in 1:8 stands against its message as applied to Job: a warning that even true-sounding revelation can be used wrongly.
views: Some readers take it as a genuine word from God, misapplied by Eliphaz.
Others see a deceiving or unnamed spirit (compare 1 Kings 22:21–23), or a parody of prophetic experience.

title: Happy Is the One God Corrects
sum: Eliphaz goes on. Job can cry out, but none of the holy ones will answer him. Resentment kills the fool: Eliphaz once saw a fool take root and suddenly declared his home cursed, his sons crushed in court and his harvest eaten by the hungry. Trouble does not sprout from the soil; humans are born to it, as sparks fly upward. So, he says, "If it were me, I would turn to God," the God who does great things beyond searching out, sends rain, lifts the lowly and catches the crafty in their own schemes.

Then comes his great promise. Happy is the man whom God corrects; do not reject the Almighty's discipline. God wounds and binds up. In six troubles, even seven, he will rescue: from famine and war, the whip of the tongue, havoc and wild beasts. Job will have peace with the stones and the animals, a safe tent, a full flock, many descendants, and a death in ripe old age like grain at harvest. "We have studied it, and that is how it is."
readings: Read as the gospel of discipline

Eliphaz's second half is one of the Bible's finest statements of hope in suffering: God disciplines because he loves, and he heals what he wounds (Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11). Many readers draw real comfort from these verses, and the book's ending, where Job is restored with children and a long life, seems to fulfill Eliphaz's promise.
Read as a hard comfort

Others hear the cruelty in the comfort: Eliphaz promises many children to a man whose ten children are dead and says the fool's sons are crushed with no one to save them. His promise of safety assumes that Job needs correcting. The LORD's final verdict (42:7) and Job's reply in chapters 6–7 show the cost of true words spoken to the wrong man at the wrong time.

views.H: The continuation of Eliphaz's real counsel to Job.
views.C: The second half of the speech, built on standard forms: a fool's fate (5:2–7), a hymn to God's power (5:9–16), a beatitude and a list of promised blessings with a numerical saying (5:17–26). The poet gives Eliphaz the most polished wisdom forms of the time.
views.W: The Babylonian Theodicy's friend, like Eliphaz, urges the sufferer to seek the god, promising that the god will show mercy. In Ludlul the sufferer is indeed restored, which fits Eliphaz's scheme; Job's ending both resembles this and differs, since the LORD rejects the friends' reasoning.
views.J: The idea of 'sufferings of love' (yissurin shel ahavah), suffering sent to the righteous out of love, is discussed in the Talmud (Bavli Berakhot 5a); Eliphaz's 5:17 is close to it. The Mishnah's 'lords of the field' appear in Rashi's comment on 5:23.
views.X: Paul quotes 5:13 in 1 Corinthians 3:19, and Hebrews 12:5–11 develops the theme of 5:17 from Proverbs 3:11–12. Christian teachers often distinguish punishment, which looks back, from discipline, which looks forward, and read Job's trial as the second.

deep.b: Eliphaz offers the kindest explanation the friends have: suffering is the Almighty's musar, his training or correction, and those who accept it are fortunate (5:17). This is a biblical teaching (Deuteronomy 8:5; Psalm 94:12; Proverbs 3:11–12), and Elihu will develop it (33:14–30; 36:8–15). But the book has already told the reader that Job's suffering is neither punishment nor correction: it is a test of whether his faith is "for no reason" (1:9; 2:3). So the book does not deny that God disciplines; it denies that discipline explains every case. That is why many readers say the friends' great fault is not their theology but their certainty: "We have studied it, and that is how it is" (5:27).

echoes: 1 Corinthians 3:19; Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11; Psalm 94:12; Deuteronomy 32:39; Hosea 6:1; Hosea 2:18; Psalm 145:3; 9:10; 42:12–17

traditions.q: Is suffering God's discipline, and should the sick expect healing?
views: Suffering can be purifying and, united with Christ, redemptive; it is not always punishment for personal sin. The Church prays for healing (the Anointing of the Sick) while teaching that suffering accepted in faith has value (Salvifici Doloris 12, 19–24; Catechism 1500–1510).
Suffering, patiently borne, is a means of healing the soul and growing toward God; Job is honored as a model of patient endurance, and the Church anoints the sick in the service of Holy Unction.
Afflictions of believers are fatherly chastisement, not punishment: God uses them to humble, correct and sanctify his children (Westminster Confession 5.5; Calvin's Sermons on Job).

Divine healing is provided in the atonement and is to be prayed for and expected (Assemblies of God Fundamental Truths 12); Pentecostals differ on how this fits cases like Job, with many affirming that God may also allow trials.

title: Friends Like a Dry Stream
sum: Job answers. If his bitterness could be weighed, it would outweigh the sand of the seas; that is why his words have been wild. The Almighty's arrows are in him and his spirit drinks their poison. A donkey does not bray when it has grass; Job cries out because something is wrong. Eliphaz's words are as tasteless as food without salt. Job wishes God would grant his one request: to crush him and cut him off. His one comfort would be that he has not hidden the words of the Holy One. He has no strength left; he is not stone or bronze.

Then he turns on his friends. A man melting away deserves loyal love from his friend, even if he lets go of the fear of the Almighty. But his brothers have failed him like a desert wadi that runs with ice in winter and is dry when the caravans of Tema and Sheba come looking for water. He never asked them for money or rescue. "Instruct me, and I will hold my tongue. Make me see what mistake I have made." They would gamble over an orphan. He asks them to look him in the face and think again: his righteousness is at stake.
readings: Read as the cry of a wounded friend

At the center of the chapter is a plea for hesed, loyal love (6:14). Job's complaint is not first that his friends are wrong about God, but that they have failed him as friends. The wadi image is one of the most vivid pictures of disappointed hope in the Bible, and many readers have found in it the measure of what comfort ought to be.
Read as the start of Job's lawsuit

Job also begins to speak in legal terms: his words are weighed on scales, he asks to be shown his error, he swears he will not lie, and he says his 'being in the right' still hangs on the case (6:29). From here the debate becomes a trial in which Job will demand a hearing with God (9; 13; 23; 31).

views.H: Job's real reply to Eliphaz, in anger and grief.
views.C: Job's first answer (6–7) has two halves: to the friends (6) and to God (7). Many scholars note how Job takes up Eliphaz's words, ka'as (5:2; 6:2), the Almighty (5:17; 6:4), and turns them back on him, a pattern of quotation and response that runs through the dialogue.
views.W: In the Babylonian Theodicy the sufferer and his friend exchange courteous but sharp speeches, the friend charging him with blasphemy, the sufferer charging the friend with not understanding. Job's attack on his friends' loyalty has a close parallel there, though Job's images, the wadi and the caravans, are his own.
views.J: Rashi and Ibn Ezra explain 6:14 in different ways: whether the one who withholds kindness forsakes the fear of God, or the despairing man deserves kindness even if he forsakes it. The rabbis valued Job's insistence that friends should not add pain to pain.
views.X: Christian readers have used 6:14 and the wadi to teach the ministry of presence and loyalty to the suffering (compare Romans 12:15; Galatians 6:2). Job's 'Instruct me, and I will hold my tongue' has been read as a model of teachable humility.

echoes: Jeremiah 15:18; Deuteronomy 32:23; Lamentations 3:12–13; Isaiah 38:12; Ruth 1:8; Proverbs 17:17; Joel 3:3; 2 Kings 4:1; 19:21

settings.to: Eliphaz, with Bildad and Zophar listening
settings.why: Job defends the wildness of his words by the weight of his suffering, repeats his wish to die, and accuses the friends of failing him in loyalty like a dry stream. He asks them to show him his error instead of scolding him, and to turn and look at him honestly. He wants friends who will stand with him, not judges.
settings.readers: First readers who had trusted their neighbors in disaster and been let down (compare Psalm 41:9; Obadiah 11) heard their own complaint. The chapter warned the comfortable that the first duty to a sufferer is loyal love, not explanation.

title: What Is a Mortal?
sum: Job continues: human life is a term of hard duty, like a soldier's or a day laborer's long day. He has been given months of nothing and nights of misery; he lies down longing for morning, and his body is covered with worms and crusted dirt. His days fly faster than a weaver's shuttle and run out without hope. Then, for the first time, he speaks to God: remember that my life is a breath; soon your eyes will look for me, and I will be gone, for no one comes up from Sheol.

So he will not keep silent. "Am I the Sea, or am I the Dragon, that you station a guard over me?" When he hopes for rest, God terrifies him with dreams. He would rather be strangled; he does not want to live forever. Turning Psalm 8 inside out, he asks what a mortal is that God makes so much of him, inspecting him every morning, never looking away long enough for him to swallow. If he has sinned, what harm has he done to the Watcher of humankind? Why not forgive him? Soon he will lie in the dust, and God will search for him, and he will not be there.
readings: Read as prayer

Chapter 7 is Job's first prayer: bitter, ironic, but addressed to God. Like the laments of the Psalms, it tells God the truth about pain and asks him to act (Psalm 39; Psalm 88). The final line, that God will come looking for Job, shows that Job still believes God cares, which is why he complains.
Read as protest

Others stress the protest: Job turns the praise of Psalm 8 into a charge of surveillance, calls God the 'watcher' of humankind, and accuses him of treating a breath of a man as the monster of chaos. Read this way, the chapter shows a faith that argues with God, a tradition that runs from Abraham (Genesis 18:25) to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 12:1).

views.H: Job's real prayer from his sickbed, describing real symptoms and sleepless nights.
views.C: The second half of Job's reply, now addressed to God. Scholars note the parody of Psalm 8 in 7:17–18 and the mythic language of Sea and Dragon in 7:12, both used with deliberate irony. Its themes, life's brevity, the hope of death and God's oppressive watch, recur in chapters 9–10 and 14.
views.W: Ludlul describes the sufferer's nights of groaning, his bed a prison and his body wasted, in terms very close to 7:3–5. The Sea and the Dragon recall the Ugaritic battles of Baal and Anat with Yam and Tunnan and Marduk's guard over Tiamat in Enuma Elish. Job uses the old myth to say God treats him as cosmic enemy.
views.J: The rabbis took 7:9 ('the one who goes down to Sheol never climbs back up') as evidence that Job denied the resurrection of the dead (Bavli Bava Batra 16a), one reason some judged him harshly. Others read the verse as describing life's end, not denying the world to come.
views.X: Christians often read 7:17 against Hebrews 2:6–8, where Psalm 8 is fulfilled in Jesus, who bore God's attention as suffering for others. Job's request for forgiveness (7:21) has been read as a longing that the gospel answers; Gregory the Great reads the chapter's 'hard service' as the Christian's warfare.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Job gives God the Accuser's job
deep.b: My own reading: in chapter 7 Job unknowingly describes God in the role the reader has seen the Accuser play. The Accuser roams the earth and inspects humans (1:7); Job calls God "you watcher of human beings" (7:20) who would "check on him each morning" (7:18) and never looks away (7:19). The Accuser set his mind on Job and tested him; Job asks why God would "set your mind on him" (7:17) and "put him to the test minute by minute" (7:18), using the very phrase the LORD used to the Accuser (1:8). Later Job will say "he holds a grudge against me" (16:9) and "with your strong hand you bear me a grudge" (30:21), using the verb satam, a close relative of satan. The reader knows what Job does not: the inspector is the Accuser, acting with God's leave. Scholars have noted the satam/satan link and the parody of Psalm 8 (Habel, Clines); reading chapter 7 as Job's unwitting portrait of the Accuser is my suggestion.

echoes: Psalm 8:4–6; Psalm 144:3–4; Hebrews 2:6–8; Psalm 39:4–13; Isaiah 40:2; Isaiah 38:12; Psalm 74:13–14; 2 Samuel 12:23; Ecclesiastes 1:2; 14:1–22

settings.to: God, addressed directly from 7:7 on, with the friends listening
settings.when: continuing his reply to Eliphaz, after appealing to his friends in chapter 6
settings.why: Job describes the misery of human life and of his own sick body, reminds God that life is a breath, refuses to keep silent, and protests that God watches and tests him as if he were the monster of chaos. He asks why God will not forgive whatever sin he may have committed before it is too late. His aim is to move God to let him go or to answer.
settings.readers: For readers whose own complaint was before God (Psalm 44; Lamentations 3), Job's prayer showed that protest addressed to God is still prayer. Its echo of Isaiah 40:2's 'hard service' and its plea for forgiveness let exiles hear their own hope in Job's mouth, sharpened by the knowledge that Job's suffering, unlike theirs, was not for sin.
